title: Who your friends are
hook: Facebook friendship patterns connect countries through shared histories and migration ties.
notes: Meta Social Connectedness Index (SCI), country level, snapshot of 25 Jan 2026 (HDX release, CC0). The SCI measures how likely two Facebook users, one in each country, are to be friends. Here it is shown relative to the median of all country pairs: 100× means a hundred times as likely as a typical pair. Because it is a per-person measure, big countries (Brazil, Mexico, Turkey, the US) score lower than small ones with the same number of friendships. It only covers Facebook users: no data for China, Iran, North Korea, Syria, Cuba, Turkmenistan, Palestine and some small territories, and countries where few people use Facebook are less reliable. Comparisons are descriptive: the index does not establish a causal effect of border policy and a multiple above one is still stronger than the median country pair.

scenes.title: Portugal's friends overseas
scenes.text: Take one person in Portugal and one in Cape Verde. They are about 2,700 times as likely to be Facebook friends as two people in a typical pair of countries. São Tomé (2,300×) and Guinea-Bissau (1,000×), also former Portuguese colonies, come next, then Luxembourg (770×), home to many Portuguese migrants. Seen from Brazil, Portugal (37×) is the closest tie of all.

scenes.title: Britain's cousins far away
scenes.text: New Zealand (36×) and Australia (33×) lie on the other side of the world, yet Britons are five to six times as connected to them as to France (6×) or the US (5×). Ireland (88×) and Caribbean islands such as St Vincent (130×) and Grenada (90×) are even closer.

scenes.title: India's Gulf
scenes.text: India's strongest ties run to the Gulf, where millions of Indians work: the UAE (38×), Kuwait (31×), Bahrain, Qatar and Oman (28–30×). That is far more than with neighbouring Pakistan (4×) or the US (0.8×).

scenes.title: Germany's guest workers
scenes.text: Germany is more connected to Kosovo (156×), North Macedonia (126×) and Bosnia (109×) than to its neighbours Austria (93×) or France (8×). The links follow decades of migration from the Balkans, Poland (25×) and Turkey (19×).

scenes.title: America looks south
scenes.text: The US's closest ties run to the Caribbean and Central America: Jamaica (64×), the Bahamas (54×), Honduras (39×), the Dominican Republic and El Salvador (31–36×). Mexico scores 13× because it is so big, but seen from Mexico, the US is its closest tie. Top of the list: Micronesia (81×), whose citizens may live and work in the US.

scenes.title: Neighbours, unequal ties
scenes.text: Neighbouring countries can have very different Facebook ties. The index measures relative friendship likelihood; it does not isolate the effects of borders, language, migration or platform use.

options.label: Armenia
options.text: Among sampled Facebook users, Armenia is much more connected to Russia (770×) and Georgia (83×) than to Azerbaijan (4×) or Turkey (1.5×). Even those weaker ties exceed the typical pair. These are relative likelihoods, not counts of friendships or evidence of a single political cause.

options.label: Greece
options.text: Greece is tightly linked to Cyprus (610×) and Albania (430×), and less strongly to Bulgaria (41×) and Turkey (4×). Neighbourhood alone does not explain the differences: the index cannot separate migration, language and other influences.

options.label: Israel
options.text: Israel’s strongest recorded ties are with Russia (53×); Jordan (49×) is also close. Egypt (4×) and Lebanon (9×) score lower. There is no data for Syria or the Palestinian territories. These comparisons cover Facebook users, not all residents or their political views.

scenes.title: Your turn
scenes.text: The Philippines, like India, is tied to the Gulf: Qatar (53×), Kuwait (50×) and the UAE (43×) top its list. Tap any country to see who its people are friends with.
